newsitem.title: UK: Cold winter forecast for U.S. Northeast, Europe.
newsitem.headline: Cold winter forecast for U.S. Northeast, Europe.

text.p: Winter weather this year in the world's biggest heating oil market, the U.S. Northeast, is likely to prove colder than normal and Europe also looks set for below average temperatures, a leading meteorologist said Monday.
A colder and weaker than normal jet stream air flow from the Pacific Ocean was likely to keep temperatures below average, said Jon Davis, chief meteorologist at brokers Smith, Barney.
"It is somewhat unlikely to be extremely cold but even less likely to be extremely warm," Davis told the annual International Herald Tribune Oil and Money Conference.
Equatorial Pacific sea temperatures were currently about one degree Centigrade below normal and likely to produce a colder than normal jet stream across the United States.
The so-called La Nina event in the Pacific was likely to be repeated this year, although temperatures were unlikely to run as low for as long as they did last winter, Davis said.
"This winter is going to be a La Nina or cold episode winter," he said.
The absence of the opposite phenomenon, warm Pacific temperatures of the El Nino affect, which produced such a mild U.S. winter in 1994/95, virtually ruled out a warm winter this year.
"We're not going to have a warm winter -- the chances of an unusually warm winter across the U.S. this winter are extremely, extremely low," Davis said.
Low stocks of heating oil in both Europe and the U.S. have helped propel world oil prices to their highest level since the Gulf War and a cold winter could add to the rally, analysts say.
The jet stream often determines U.S. winter weather by determining the flow of warm air across the continent and the volume of cold air allowed to penetrate from the Arctic.
Davis said the chances of a repeat of last year's extremely severe winter, kicked off by an early November cold snap, were fairly low.
"The bulk of the extreme cold will come in the middle to latter part of the winter," he said.
Davis said European winter temperatures were likely to prove colder than normal.
"The bias is for colder than normal this winter in Europe especially in the early/middle season," he said.
A warm pocket of water in the western Atlantic, not seen for 15 years, would force the jet stream north and send colder air into Europe.
Expectations for a weaker jet stream will also allow cold Arctic air to flow more easily into Europe, he added.
